article.overview: Electrical conductivity describes how easily an electric current passes through a material. In the regolith, it depends on how much water or ice is present, how porous the material is, how it is packed, and how it is layered. The Apollo 17 SEP report states that minute amounts of water in rocks or subsoil change the electrical conductivity by several orders of magnitude, which is why electrical measurements are sensitive to moisture [1]. Only one lunar in-situ electrical-properties experiment was found among the sources consulted: the Apollo 17 SEP. It was flown at Taurus-Littrow in December 1972. It transmitted radio waves from the surface at frequencies from 1 to 32 MHz and used interference between waves travelling above and below the surface to infer the layering of the subsurface [1][2]. A 2018 reanalysis of the SEP data by Grimm presents a depth model for the upper crust at that site [3]. Electrode-type probes have been flown on Mars. The Phoenix Thermal and Electrical Conductivity Probe (TECP) measured electrical conductivity and permittivity in Martian soil in 2008, using pairs of needles as electrodes [7]. Newer designs for lunar and planetary use are in development. These include a JPL electrical properties probe, which was built and tested in the laboratory, and a permittivity sensor developed at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). None of these newer designs has been reported as flown [4][5].
article.scope: Scope chosen for this payload: in-situ instruments whose main product is the electrical conductivity of regolith, measured in place, including permittivity where the same instrument reports it. Included are electrode and needle probes pushed into or onto the soil and active radio-frequency surface sounding experiments (Apollo 17 SEP). Excluded or cross-referenced: thermal conductivity probes (payload 010, which share hardware with the Phoenix TECP); electrical resistivity probes (payload 090, reciprocal quantity); natural-source electromagnetic induction sounding of the interior (payload 021, magnetotelluric sounder); general electromagnetic field sensing (payload 020). The Apollo 17 SEP lies near the boundary with payloads 020 and 021 because it is an active surface experiment rather than a probe.
article.description: An electrical conductivity probe applies a known electrical signal to the soil and measures the response, which is converted into conductivity using the electrode geometry and the signal frequency. Three measurement styles appear in the sources read. In the first, electrodes on a rod, needle or cylinder measure the impedance between them, as in the JPL Electrical Properties Probe and the Phoenix TECP. In the second, a flat electrode forms a capacitor with the soil, and the measured capacitance gives the soil's effective relative permittivity, as in the TUM permittivity sensor [4][5][7]. In the third, the instrument is not inserted into the soil: dipole antennas on the surface transmit radio waves, a receiver measures the fields at a distance, and interference between waves travelling above and below the surface is used to infer the electrical properties with depth, as in the Apollo 17 SEP [1][2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of an electrical conductivity measurement is to determine how the subsurface conducts electricity, and from that to infer composition, moisture and structure. The Apollo 17 SEP report describes its aim as obtaining data on the transmission, absorption and reflection of electromagnetic energy by the lunar surface and subsurface, for a geological model of the upper layers of the Moon. The experiment was designed to determine layering, to search for water below the surface, and to measure electrical properties in situ as a function of depth, from a few metres to a few kilometres [1]. A second application is detection of water or ice. The JPL probe's design goal is detection of water or ice at about 0.1 weight per cent [5]. The TUM permittivity sensor is intended to support water-content mapping, but its water-resolution target of 1 per cent is not yet met [4]. A third application is support for electrical models of the interior, which links to payloads 009, 010 and 021. A surface probe cannot see deep structure directly, so its value lies in characterising the shallow layers that deeper methods must account for.
article.operating_principle: Electrode probes apply an alternating voltage to electrodes and measure the resulting current. The ratio gives an impedance with a magnitude and a phase angle. For a known electrode geometry, the resistive part of the impedance relates to the soil conductivity between the electrodes. The JPL probe reports impedance magnitude and phase across 20 Hz to 500 kHz [5]. The sources read do not give explicit calibration equations for each instrument, so no general conversion formula is given here. Capacitive permittivity sensing uses a flat electrode that forms a capacitor with the soil. The TUM sensor records a voltage time series under square-wave excitation, converts it to the frequency domain with a Fourier transform, fits the capacitance from the Fourier coefficients, and derives effective relative permittivity [4]. The Apollo 17 SEP used continuous-wave transmission at 1, 2.4, 4, 8.1, 16 and 32.1 MHz, one after another, and recorded field strength as a function of distance. The PDS description states that the waves permitted measurement of the size and number of scattered bodies in the subsurface [1]. The 1974 final report describes radio-frequency interferometry, in which the receiver records the pattern formed by waves travelling above and below the surface [2]. A 2018 reanalysis interprets the signal decay as mainly absorption, with little small-scale scattering, and derives loss tangents of about 0.01 [3]. The reanalysis results are taken from search summaries of the paper, not from its full text.
article.scientific_importance: The Apollo 17 SEP is the only flown lunar example in this article. Its importance lies in showing that the electrical properties of the lunar subsurface can be measured from the surface, to depths far greater than a conventional probe can reach. The 1972 instrument is known through its published reports, and its 2018 reanalysis gives a depth model. The reanalysis derived a porosity that falls sharply in the top 20 to 30 m, changes little below 300 m, and reflects a transition from regolith to fractured rock and then to intact basalt. It also reports that the bottom of the basalt was not detected to a depth of about 2 km or more [3]. These are interpretations of data from a single site. Electrode probes and permittivity sensors are important because they give in-situ values for the top layers of the soil, where most of the interaction with water and ice takes place. The Phoenix TECP is the flown electrode-type example in this article. Its electrical measurements are of conductivity and permittivity, and they complement the thermal measurements described in payload 010 [7].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, frequency range or power for an electrical conductivity probe. The designs below use different geometries, frequency ranges and measurement quantities, and their outputs are not directly comparable. Values are given only for the named instrument and source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the article says so and no value has been inferred.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Surface Electrical Properties (SEP) experiment

examples.transmitter: Deployable self-contained transmitter with a multiple-frequency transmitter antenna; the crew set it up about 100 m from the Lunar Module and deployed the antennas [1]
examples.transmitting_antennas: Two orthogonal, horizontal electric dipole antennas on the lunar surface [2]

examples.receiver: Wide-bandwidth receiver with three orthogonal, electrically small loops measuring field strength as a function of distance [2]. The PDS document describes a portable receiver/recorder on the Lunar Roving Vehicle and also states that the receiver/recorder was placed on the Lunar Module; the document does not reconcile these [1]
examples.measurement_geometry: Crew established the location of the LRV relative to the transmitter at each data stop; wheel turns and navigation azimuth gave distances [1]
examples.depth_range: Selected frequency range chosen to probe from a few metres to a few kilometres of depth [1]
examples.data_recording: Data recorded on magnetic tape and returned to Earth [2]; the PDS description refers to a retrievable data recording device [1]
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the sources read
examples.power: Not stated in the sources read

examples.name: JPL Electrical Properties Probe (NPO-44261)
examples.status: Designed as a prototype of instruments for measuring liquid-water and ice contents of lunar and planetary soils; built and tested in the laboratory; not flown [5]
examples.geometry: Two electrodes in a compact assembly near the tip of a cylinder; the electrodes protrude slightly from the cylinder. No numerical protrusion, cylinder diameter or cylinder length given [5]
examples.method: Impedance measurement; magnitude and phase angle across 20 Hz to 500 kHz; typical run takes several seconds; the cylinder is pushed into the ground; no sample handling [5]
examples.detection: Water or ice presence detectable at about 0.1 weight per cent; concentration measurable above 0.5 weight per cent (body text) [5]
examples.laboratory_tests: Tests from -25 to +65 degrees C on dry silica sand and on silica sand moistened with 0.1 weight per cent of a 0.1 M KCl solution. The test material was not lunar regolith or a lunar simulant [5]
examples.lineage: Improves on NPO-41822, an earlier design that used a sample jar and an impedance spectrometer [5]
examples.conductivity_note: The Tech Brief overview claims conductivity and dielectric-constant measurement; the body text reports impedance magnitude and phase only [5]
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the source read
examples.power: Not stated in the source read
examples.qualification: Laboratory prototype. The Tech Brief overview ('25 °C to -65 °C') and body ('-25 to +65 °C') give conflicting temperature ranges, both confirmed in the saved page in this run; the body text values are used. The original NASA technical support package requires a login and was not read.

examples.name: TUM permittivity sensor (flat patch electrode)
examples.status: Built and tested in the laboratory; no flight testing reported; TRL not stated; a TRL of 6 is planned 'within the next year' [4]
examples.sensor: Capacitive permittivity sensor with a flat patch electrode forming an RC circuit with the sample; two-layer printed circuit board with signal, ground and guard electrodes [4]
examples.geometry: Hardware side length 6.5 cm; simulations use a 60 mm electrode diameter, treated as a separate reference. The two values are not reconciled in the text [4]
examples.excitation_and_frequency: Square-wave excitation; frequencies from 6.25 Hz to 10 kHz; baseline sampling rate 20 kHz; excitation switching frequency 12.5 Hz in experiments [4]
examples.derived_quantities: Capacitance, effective relative permittivity, and porosity and water content inferred with a power-law mixing model. Water content is the goal and is not validated quantitatively. Conductivity is mentioned in the introduction but not reported [4]
examples.calibration_and_tests: Calibration against known capacitors with a stated 10 per cent nominal uncertainty (linear fit r-squared 0.997). Tests with quartz sand and JSC-1A lunar regolith simulant at atmospheric pressure from -40 to 40 degrees C, five repeats per measurement [4]
examples.sensing_depth: Simulated sensing depth about 5 cm for the 60 mm electrode, using a 10 per cent potential-decay criterion [4]
examples.water_resolution_status: Intended resolution of 1 per cent for water not yet met; the sensor needs to be reduced to achieve it [4]
examples.mass_note: Total system weight 18 g given in the sensor description. The discussion says the current system weighs below 100 g including the harness. The paper does not reconcile these values [4]
examples.dimensions: Side length 6.5 cm (hardware description); see geometry note
examples.power: About 1.5 W average for the non-optimised back-end electronics [4]
examples.data_volume: About 570 kbyte per 2 s measurement in the methods; about 500 kbyte in the discussion [4]
examples.thermal_test_range: Electronics operated from -40 to 60 degrees C in tests [4]
examples.qualification: Laboratory development. No flight testing reported. Predicted vs measured capacitance examples are in the paper (JSC-1A 9.34 pF vs 12.70 pF; granite 13.17 pF vs 20.81 pF; air 4.13 pF vs 5.02 pF) [4].

examples.name: TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor (RPS)
examples.status: Pre-flight development. Launch planned no earlier than 2029 on the MBRSC Rashid-3 rover. No flight hardware described [6]
examples.sensor: Two electrodes of different sizes mounted on a rover wheel; slip ring to front-end electronics in the rover body; each electrode has an integrated resistive temperature detector; a separate infrared thermopile views the undisturbed regolith [6]
examples.quantity: Electrical permittivity of lunar regolith; water content is an application goal, not a direct measurement; conductivity not mentioned [6]
examples.method: Square-wave excitation at several frequencies; no frequency values given [6]
examples.depth: Electrode dimensions set the maximum measurement depth; no numerical depth given [6]
examples.qualification: Pre-flight. Page is labelled last updated 07/2025 but cites 2026 publications and includes 2026-dated images; status should be checked with the group before reuse [6].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo 17 SEP was a surface-deployed antenna array with a transmitter about 100 m from the Lunar Module; the laboratory and flight electrode probes are small cylinders or needles with electrodes at their tips or faces. Dimensions for the flown SEP hardware and the JPL probe are not stated in the sources read. The TUM hardware has a stated 6.5 cm electrode side length, with a 60 mm simulated electrode diameter. The TECP needle length is 15 mm [1][4][5][7][8].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only stated mass in this article is the TUM sensor's total system weight of 18 g in its sensor description, with a discussion value of below 100 g including the harness; these values are not reconciled [4]. Mass for the Apollo 17 SEP, the TECP, the JPL probe and the TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor is not stated in the sources read. Mass determines launch and lander requirements, so no mass is inferred for any of these instruments.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The TUM back-end electronics use about 1.5 W average (non-optimised) [4]. Power for the Apollo 17 SEP, the TECP, the JPL probe and the TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor is not stated in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Electrical measurements depend on the contact between sensor and soil. Electrode probes must be inserted or pressed into the regolith, and poor insertion degrades the measurement, as reported for the Phoenix TECP [7]. Surface antenna experiments depend on antenna geometry and on the transmitter-receiver distance, which the Apollo 17 crew recorded at each stop [1]. Temperature affects both electronics and soil: the JPL probe was tested from -25 to +65 degrees C [5]; the TUM sensor electronics operated from -40 to 60 degrees C and the laboratory measurements covered -40 to 40 degrees C [4]. The lunar surface experiences much larger temperature swings, and the sources read do not test an electrode probe over the full lunar surface temperature cycle. Moisture is the property being measured, so the instrument must separate the moisture signal from the signal due to soil structure and packing. The TUM water-resolution target of 1 per cent is not yet met [4], and the JPL probe's laboratory detection threshold is about 0.1 weight per cent on sand [5]. Power and data needs depend on design: the TUM back end uses about 1.5 W and produces hundreds of kilobytes per measurement [4]. The Apollo 17 SEP recorded data on tape and returned it to Earth [2].
article.limitations: No flown lunar in-situ electrical conductivity probe is described in the sources consulted. The only lunar example, the Apollo 17 SEP, is an active radio-frequency sounding experiment at one site and not a probe [1][2]. Its 2018 reanalysis is one interpretation among possible models [3]. Electrical methods are sensitive to contact, geometry and moisture. Electrode probes measure a small volume near the electrodes and depend on calibration and modelled geometry. The TUM sensor's simulated sensing depth is about 5 cm [4]. Conductivity and permittivity are different quantities, and the TUM sensor and the JPL probe do not report conductivity in their results [4][5]. Laboratory results were obtained on silica sand, JSC-1A simulant or quartz sand at atmospheric pressure, not on lunar regolith in vacuum [4][5]. The TECP results come from Mars, where soil and atmosphere differ from the lunar environment [7].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: An electrical conductivity probe may be delivered to the Moon as a dedicated instrument or as part of a larger surface package. Transport and deployment requirements depend strongly on the design: an antenna experiment needs a transmitter and receiver placed at known distances, while a probe needs insertion into or contact with the regolith.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument or its transmitter, receiver and antennas with the lander or rover on Earth.
Launch it and transfer it towards the Moon.
Deliver it to the surface by lander, or mount it on a rover.
Deploy the antennas or insert the electrodes, and establish the geometry relative to the lander or rover.
Connect the power and data interfaces, and recover or transmit the data.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 17 SEP was carried and set up by the astronauts. The crew transported the transmitter, set it up about 100 m from the Lunar Module, deployed the antennas, and then recorded the rover position at each stop during the traverse [1]. The TECP needles were inserted into the Martian soil; the insertion mechanism is not described in the sources read [7]. The TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor is designed for a wheel-mounted configuration on the Rashid-3 rover, with a slip ring transferring the electrode signal from the rotating wheel to the rover body [6]. Stowage, mechanical loads and the rover interface are not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 17 SEP (crew-deployed antenna array with a rover-mounted receiver, December 1972) [1][2]. Phoenix TECP (needle probe inserted into Martian soil, 2008) [7][8]. These are historical examples of deployment methods and are not evidence of how a future instrument would be delivered.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lunar lander, rover or spacecraft is assessed for compatibility with an electrical conductivity probe. Mass, dimensions, mounting, deployment loads, power and data interfaces would need to be compared with verified lander specifications. The sources read do not name the lander or launch vehicle for the Rashid-3 rover, so no interface is assumed for the TUM sensor [6].

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 SEP was the only lunar in-situ electrical-properties experiment identified in this research run. It showed that radio-frequency sounding from the surface could infer electrical layering of the lunar subsurface [1][2]. Its 2018 reanalysis produced a depth model for the upper crust at Taurus-Littrow [3]. The Phoenix TECP measured soil electrical properties on Mars in 2008, using electrodes in the soil [7]. The JPL and TUM developments show continuing effort to make such probes suitable for lunar and planetary soils, although neither has been reported as flown [4][5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flown lunar in-situ electrical conductivity probe is described in the sources consulted. The only lunar example is the Apollo 17 SEP, which is an active radio-frequency sounding experiment at one site, not a probe. Its results are interpretations of 1972 data, and the 2018 reanalysis is one interpretation among several possible models [1][2][3]. Electrical methods are sensitive to contact, geometry and moisture. Electrode probes measure a small volume of soil near the electrodes, so they must be positioned correctly, and their results depend on the calibration and the modelled geometry. The sensing depth of the TUM sensor is about 5 cm for the simulated electrode [4]. Conductivity and permittivity are different quantities, and an instrument that reports one may not report the other. The TUM sensor and the JPL probe do not report conductivity in the results [4][5]. The laboratory results were obtained on silica sand, JSC-1A lunar regolith simulant, or quartz sand, at atmospheric pressure. They were not obtained on lunar regolith in vacuum [4][5]. The TECP results come from Mars, where the soil and atmosphere differ from the lunar environment [7]. Evidence gaps: the Apollo 17 SEP frequencies differ between the PDS instrument description (1, 2.4, 4, 8.1, 16 and 32.1 MHz) and the NTRS record summary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 MHz), and the PDS values are used; the PDS document places the receiver both on the LRV and on the Lunar Module, which is not reconciled [1]; the 1974 MIT final report (NTRS 19750013120) was not readable as text in this run, and the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report chapter 15 was not read [2]; the Grimm (2018) full text was not accessible, so its loss tangent, porosity profile and basalt depth come from search summaries [3]; TECP excitation, measurement range, accuracy, duration, mass and power are not stated in the sources read, and the Zent et al. (2009) paper was not read [7]; the JPL Tech Brief gives conflicting temperature ranges and claims conductivity measurement that its body does not report, and the original support package was not read [5]; the TUM permittivity sensor's mass, data-size and electrode-size figures are inconsistent within the paper [4]; the TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor page is labelled 07/2025 but cites 2026 items [6]; no verified photograph of a lunar conductivity probe was identified. This article does not recommend lunar landing sites or locations; that is deferred by the user.

data_quality_notes: Scope: electrical conductivity probes (in-situ, regolith, measured in place), including permittivity where the same instrument reports it. Included: electrode and needle probes and the active radio-frequency surface sounding experiment Apollo 17 SEP. Cross-referenced, not repeated: thermal conductivity probe (payload 010, shared hardware with the Phoenix TECP), electrical resistivity probe (payload 090), magnetotelluric sounder (payload 021), electromagnetic field sensor (payload 020).

Only one lunar in-situ electrical-properties experiment (Apollo 17 SEP) was identified in the sources consulted. The SEP is an active surface radio-frequency experiment, not a penetrating probe, and sits near the boundaries with payloads 020 and 021.
Apollo 17 SEP frequencies differ between sources: PDS instrument description 1, 2.4, 4, 8.1, 16, 32.1 MHz; NTRS record summary 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 MHz. The PDS values are used.
Apollo 17 SEP receiver location is inconsistent within the PDS document (portable receiver/recorder on the LRV versus receiver/recorder placed on the LM). Not reconciled.

Apollo 17 SEP mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the sources read. The 1974 MIT final report (NTRS 19750013120) was located, but its scanned PDF has no readable text layer in this run, so its hardware and results sections were not read. The Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report chapter 15 was not read.

Grimm (2018) Icarus reanalysis: the DOI resolves (HTTP 200 in this run), but the full text was not accessed. The loss tangent (about 0.01), porosity profile (sharp change in top 20-30 m) and basalt-depth statement (not detected to about 2 km or more) come from search summaries and must be checked against the article before reuse.

Phoenix TECP: electrical functions taken from the MECA help page. Excitation frequency or waveform, measurement range and accuracy, duration, mass and power are not stated in the sources read. The Zent et al. (2009) TECP paper was not read. Needle length of 15 mm (0.6 inch) is stated on the JPL Photojournal page PIA11722, confirmed in this run.

JPL Electrical Properties Probe (NPO-44261): laboratory prototype, not flown. The Tech Brief page gives conflicting temperature ranges (overview '25 °C to -65 °C'; body '-25 to +65 °C'); both were confirmed in the saved page and the body values are used. The overview claims conductivity and dielectric-constant measurement that the body does not report. Original technical support package requires a login and was not read. Tests were on silica sand, not lunar regolith.

TUM permittivity sensor (Gscheidle et al. 2024): laboratory development, not flown, TRL not stated (planned TRL 6 within the next year). Conductivity mentioned in the introduction but not reported. Mass is given as 18 g total system weight in one place and below 100 g including the harness in another; electrode is 6.5 cm side length in hardware and 60 mm diameter in simulations; data size differs between sections. These inconsistencies are reported, not resolved.

TUM Rover Permittivity Sensor: pre-flight development, launch planned no earlier than 2029 on the MBRSC Rashid-3 rover per the TUM project page. The page is labelled last updated 07/2025 but cites 2026 publications and includes 2026-dated images; status should be verified with the group. No accuracy, mass, dimensions, power or frequency values are published on the page.
